messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir was seventy-five years old, a sculptor who had spent half a lifetime shaping marble and granite into forms that seemed to breathe. The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in his studio. He had been reaching for a fine chisel on a high shelf, the concrete floor slick with clay slurry from a morning of shaping a human figure. His foot slipped. He fell backward, his skull striking the edge of a rough-hewn block of Carrara marble with a sound that he would later describe as the world cracking open. He was found unconscious by a delivery driver an hour later. At the hospital, a subdural hematoma required emergency surgery. He survived, but the recovery was slow, and something in the way he inhabited his own body never returned.

In the months that followed, Amir became certain that his body was no longer a reliable instrument. He had always trusted it—the steady hand, the measured breath, the controlled strength needed to chisel against stone for hours. Now he felt fragile, hollowed out, as if the accident had introduced a permanent flaw. He could no longer shake the conviction that he had been permanently changed for the worse, that his flesh and bones were now dangerously vulnerable. These thoughts were not fleeting; they settled into his bones as facts. The scar on his scalp and the occasional blurring of his left eye confirmed what he already knew: his body had been damaged beyond repair, and he could not count on it not to betray him again.

Because he came to view his own body as treacherous, Amir began to watch it with relentless vigilance. Throughout the day, he would stop mid-task and press two fingers to his wrist, counting his pulse, feeling for an irregularity. He would strain his neck to check for stiffness that might signal a coming stroke. He avoided any physical exertion that put his system under stress—no more climbing stepladders, no heavy lifting, no leaning over a large block for more than a few minutes. He had always worked standing; now he sat. He stopped accepting commissions for large-scale pieces, telling himself he was simply being careful. He also found himself turning over the accident again and again, searching for reasons: *Why did this happen to me? Was I meant to be punished? Did I ignore some warning?* This relentless meaning-seeking filled his quiet hours, a mental loop that offered no answer but which he could not stop.

These strategies reshaped his life. His studio, once a space of physical abandon and creative risk, became a place where every step was calculated. He worked only with small clay maquettes, objects he could rotate on a turntable without strain. His children, who visited on weekends, noticed he no longer offered to carry his granddaughters onto his lap—he was afraid his arms would fail. He declined invitations to group exhibitions, worried that standing in a gallery would cause his back to seize. The vibrancy of his art had muted; the forms were still beautiful, but smaller, contained, as though they shared his fear of taking up space. He had always prided himself on producing a dozen major works a year; in the last twelve months he had finished two.

What finally brought Amir to seek help was the silence of his studio. He had not touched a tool in three weeks. He would walk to the door, look at the clay, and turn away, exhausted by the internal arithmetic of risk. He had come to believe that his body was permanently broken, and that the only way to protect himself was to retreat further. But he also knew that retreat was slowly erasing him. He was most afraid of never sculpting again—of becoming a man who only waited for his body to fail. And yet, as he sat across from me, he could not stop himself from quietly pressing his thumb against his own ribcage, feeling for a heartbeat he already knew was there.
